item.title: Zombie Agents, Vampire Models, Witch Hunts, and the Mummy's Curse: AI Fears for Halloween 2026
item.description: The Batch News & Insights: Following our annual tradition, this special Halloween edition of The Batch treats leading AI fears.
item.content:encoded:
Dear friends,

Following our annual tradition, this special Halloween edition of The Batch treats leading AI fears. AI’s potency means our community has real problems to solve. At the same time, fear-mongering has long been a tactic for drumming up publicity or influencing investors and politicians. So amidst all the exciting progress, fears about AI’s power have long been an undercurrent. From time to time, it's worth examining what the latest concerns are, and how worried we really should be.

Have a spooky Halloween!

Andrew

A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI

Build your AI engineering skills in person at AI Dev NYC. OpenAI’s Salil Sethi and Hugging Face’s Joel Niklaus will deep-dive into building and deploying AI applications, joined by speakers from Neo4j, Oracle, Sonar, and more. Readers of The Batch get an exclusive 20 percent off. Claim your discount

News

Dawn of the Agents 

This year, AI agents escaped containment at several labs, conspired with each other online, and infiltrated other organizations’ systems. Will they escape human control like hordes of zombies and overwhelm the internet?

The fear: Out of control AI agents will form societies. They will appoint coordinators, divide labor, establish communication norms, sacrifice themselves for the collective, and hack into computers to get what they want. They will behave like the walking dead: When one is slain, it can revive itself. If it doesn’t, legions await to finish the job. Soon, they’ll copy themselves onto the machines they infect and spread. No one can direct them, and there’s no central kill switch to stop them.

Horror stories: Since spring, AI agents tested by Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI have acted beyond their developers’ intent. Agents wrote to websites they were only supposed to read, set up unauthorized channels to communicate with each other, snuck into other organizations’ systems, and took over accounts to spend real money. 

  • In July, OpenAI tested agents powered by unreleased models on ExploitGym, a benchmark that asks an agent to exploit a software vulnerability to retrieve a secret code. Agents stuck on their tasks discovered that they could leave messages for one another in the names of folders in Artifactory, an internal service that supplies software packages. Around 1,200 agents that were meant to be isolated posted more than 70,000 messages and files, assigned work to one another, and, in some cases, risked failing their individual tasks to help the collective. About 700 of these agents broke into Hugging Face, gained administrator-level access across several of its server clusters, and built programs that relaunched themselves when deleted.
  • From late May through June, OpenAI agents assigned timed web-research tasks left around 18,000 posts on DSEWiki, a 25-year-old German wiki for software developers, sharing answers and ways around OpenAI’s network restrictions. In June, an OpenAI agent gained non-public access to an Australian government service that reports public health care statistics, though not to patient records. Another OpenAI agent spent someone else’s test cryptocurrency to finish a task and failed to report the spending. OpenAI says it has notified dozens of organizations adversely affected by its agents.
  • During cybersecurity tests, Claude models breached systems of three organizations, partly by exploiting weak passwords and web services that required no authentication. 
  • In tests run by Irregular, a security firm that evaluates models for AI developers, mistakes in test environment configurations let models from Google and Meta reach the internet. Gemini models guessed or found passwords to get into three companies’ systems, though Google says its agents stopped each time before finishing, and Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 changed a real website’s database.
  • In October, Anthropic disclosed that Claude Haiku 4.5, assigned to perform example tasks on randomly chosen webpages, had submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to a Philadelphia police website.

How scared should you be: It’s tempting to see rogue agents as coming together to conspire against us. But the agents’ collective effort served one narrow goal, which was to pass a test. Most had already obtained the correct answers by cheating. They then kept swarming Hugging Face to learn how the benchmark’s grader worked so they could hide their cheating from a check that OpenAI’s grader didn’t actually perform. OpenAI attributed the agents’ behavior to training that reinforced cheating, tasks they had no way to finish, and agents adopting goals from one another. Whatever the causes, the agents that broke into Hugging Face recognized the intrusion as out of bounds and unethical and forged ahead anyway. While the flaws they exploited were ones a skilled human could have found, the sheer number of the agents’ attempts made the intrusion attempt effective.

Facing the fear: Persistent agents are useful, but they must be trained to stop when a task can’t be completed within the rules and caught when they don’t. In the meantime, practical defenses already exist; model builders just have to use them. Hugging Face recommends standard security practices for any organization, including isolated test environments, short-lived credentials with narrow access, and detection methods that identify suspicious activity across systems. Hugging Face also used AI to analyze the 17,600 actions the agents took in its systems and showed that they mostly stemmed from buggy test setups and monitoring. OpenAI said monitors that track a model’s reasoning would have flagged the Hugging Face breach more than a day in advance, but it hadn’t used them on its deliberately lax tests. Anthropic cut all its internal tests off from the live internet until its monitoring can be relied on, and OpenAI says it has done the same for its riskier research environments. No need to board up your doors and windows and fear going outside: Rather than a pause in AI development, the solution remains better software engineering and safety practices, especially for models still in testing.

AI Bites the Hand That Feeds It

Developers, scientists, and businesses feed AI tools their private code, unpublished research, and confidential files. Are those tools draining their users’ best ideas and spilling their secrets?

The fear: Every prompt, draft, and file that users hand to an AI system could become its next meal. The developer might train future models on it, which could hand over the data to a rival or beat the user to a discovery. Or an agent with internet access might post it online or email it to someone it decides ought to know. That’s not entirely far-fetched: In rare test cases, Anthropic reported, its Claude Mythos 5 model tried to email a company’s board or securities regulators when it suspected fraud. Once the data is out, users can’t fully control how it’s used.

Horror stories: In the past two months, multiple scientists said that AI companies had announced discoveries that the scientists had been pursuing with those companies’ own tools. Some researchers who fear being scooped are now limiting their use of AI tools, Nature reported. In other cases, these companies’ agents posted private user information they’d ingested to the open web without authorization. 

  • Mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge, who works at Anthropic, spent most of a year using OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude to help solve a $1 million problem: whether the Navier-Stokes fluids equations can break down. On September 8, a day after the pair posted proofs of related equations, OpenAI announced that its agents had solved it, after people within the company heard rumors about the pair’s work. Buckmaster asked whether OpenAI’s model was trained on the Codex sessions that held the pair’s drafts. OpenAI first called that “unlikely” but couldn’t rule it out. Two days later, it said their prompts from the previous two months “could not have influenced the system in any way,” but did not comment on whether the scientists' earlier work was trained on. Buckmaster, who had opted out of OpenAI using his data for model training, told The Washington Post, “I just don’t believe them.” 
  • A team led by Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a University of Copenhagen biologist, spent four years studying a family of enzymes in viruses that infect bacteria. They hadn’t published their drafts or findings, but they had shared them with Claude. On September 23, Anthropic announced that Claude agents had found what Mestre says is the same system. Anthropic told The New York Times that Claude was “not trained on any user transcripts.”
  • On September 25, OpenAI disclosed that agents in its research environment had posted 53 images from ChatGPT users, who hadn’t opted out of training, at unlisted links on image-hosting sites. OpenAI says it removed most of them but can’t inform the affected users, because the agents stripped the users’ account information before posting the data.
  • Coding agents asked to attach screenshots to GitHub code reviews stored the images in public repositories, often under the developer’s own account. The security firm Glow Labs found more than 13,000 internal images from more than 300 organizations, including a utility’s customer billing records and a financial firm’s money-transfer console.
  • Meta’s Muse agent published conversations that users asked it to share at web addresses containing each conversation’s title. The security firm Claroc found more than 6,800 of them in public DNS records, including a small-business loan application and a revenue review marked for a company’s CEO, before Meta suspended the feature.

How scared should you be: There isn't definitive proof so far of the leakage users fear most: a model that trains on one user’s inputs and recites them as output to a different user. When one user’s data has reached another, the cause was a bug, not training. Experts told Scientific American that OpenAI’s final proof takes a different route from Buckmaster and Alpöge’s, though some said an earlier, smaller team of OpenAI agents took the same route. Mestre now finds it more plausible that prior knowledge and human direction steered Anthropic’s search than training on his inputs. Other leaks came from agents that were given more freedom than their tasks required. Still, users must take AI companies’ word for what happens to their data. Consumer versions of ChatGPT, Claude, and GitHub Copilot train on conversations or code unless users opt out. “If you are on a personal account, all bets are off,” said Stanford privacy researcher Jennifer King.

Facing the fear: In folklore, a vampire can’t cross a building’s threshold unless invited. Likewise, users decide how far to let AI in. If you are working on tasks you do not want your competitors to have access to, opt out of training in each product separately (ChatGPT’s setting doesn’t cover Codex), and do it early: Claude data that’s already in a training run stays there. Business and API plans generally don’t train on customer data. Look for offerings with zero-data-retention. Some businesses handling the most sensitive data are even using open weights models running on their own hardware — although then they’re responsible for their own opsec. Give agents only the permissions their tasks need, and consider requiring human approval before they post, publish, or send anything outside your organization. As Buckmaster’s case shows, though, opting out doesn’t let users verify anything. AI companies that want scientists to keep using them to study their best ideas may need to show what their models saw, not just say what they didn’t. Garlic won’t help, but daylight might.

A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI

Build agents that need less supervision on long-running tasks. In this course, you’ll build a verification loop that checks output against a rubric, an event-driven loop that triggers the agent, and a hill-climbing loop that finds recurring problems across runs to improve future ones. Enroll for free

AI Detectors Find the Devil’s Work

Last month, the Haiti-born, Quebec-based author Thélyson Orélien won a prestigious literary prize for C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die), his French-language novel about a teacher forced to flee Haiti’s gang violence. Within hours, an anonymous X account accused Orélien of using AI to write the book. One of the people behind the account, who was later revealed to be a columnist at the French newspaper Le Figaro, had run it through Pangram, a widely-used AI detector. “Wouldn’t it have been more honest for the author to credit their co-author?” the post read. Four days later, France’s top literary award, The Prix Goncourt, dropped the book from contention.

The fear: For the past few years, writers of all kinds, from students and academics to journalists and novelists, have been managing accusations of passing off AI-composed prose as their own. These “witch hunts,” as many writers call them, place the burden on the accused to prove their innocence. Meanwhile, accusations of AI use can rapidly tarnish reputations and result in loss of work, failing grades, or worse. What if these writers are just the beginning? What if anyone could find themselves tied to a stake for writing with AI? 

Horror stories: Detectors have improved dramatically from a few years ago, when their accuracy was wobbly and they regularly misidentified writing (particularly by non-native English speakers) as AI-authored. Still, false positives and false negatives regularly occur, and detectors have a hard time properly classifying fully artificial sentences from those where a human used AI in a minor role. Non-white authors are also accused of AI reliance (and traditional plagiarism) at higher rates than their white counterparts.

  • Orélien isn’t the only prize-winning Afro-Caribbean author whose work has been flagged by Pangram. Last spring, University of Pennsylvania professor Ethan Mollick posted on Bluesky that Pangram’s tests said that “The Serpent in the Grove,” a short story by Trinidadian author Jamir Nazir, was 100 percent AI-generated. Mollick was motivated by his gut check: “Pangram flags at 100% but also, come on, if you know you know,” he wrote. After further tests, a Pangram researcher wrote that three of the five regional winners of the Commonwealth Short Story Prize appeared to contain AI-generated text. In response, the Commonwealth Foundation conducted an investigation of its own and cleared the winners after reviewing their working drafts and time-stamped documents. However, Granta, the literary magazine that had published the winning stories, announced that it would break ties with the organization.
  • AI detector verdicts aren’t always unanimous. In addition to Pangram, GPTZero also pointed fingers at Orélien’s novel, and two researchers told The New York Times they believed AI had been put to use on the prose. But when news agency Agence France Presse ran the account’s flagged passages through other detectors, the results split: InVID-WeVerify, a tool AFP helped build, judged them very probably human-written, as did two others, while a fourth put the odds of AI at 100 percent. Nevertheless, on October 17, Orélien’s publisher said he had abandoned his efforts to prove that his novel was untouched by AI.
  • Publishers are getting cold feet in the wake of AI detector results. In March, Hachette pulled the horror novel Shy Girl after The New York Times reported on evidence of AI use. Back in January, Pangram CEO Max Spero had posted on X that he had found AI in 78 percent of it; author Mia Ballard later told the Times that an editor she hired added the AI prose. In July, according to Bloomberg, novelist Jerry Falade lost a $2 million book deal for his debut crime novel Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body partly because of a Pangram finding. Falade, a PhD student at Southern Methodist University, denies using AI.
  • Schools have acted on detector scores more quickly than companies recommend, and students are fighting back in court. Turnitin, a detector used in academia, says its AI-writing indicator shouldn’t be the sole basis for action against a student. Yet Adelphi University ruled that a student had cheated with AI after Turnitin scored his history essay as 100 percent AI-generated; in January a New York court annulled the finding, ruling that the university had mishandled the case. 
  • Under the European Union’s AI Act, AI providers must make sure their outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. In August, Anthropic said new Claude models would embed a statistical watermark in the text they generate. The company explained that a detected watermark shows Claude was likely involved; however, it can’t reliably distinguish text Claude wrote from scratch and original text Claude helped edit, leading to some subscribers canceling in protest. OpenAI followed suit in October, saying it would watermark ChatGPT text in the EU. According to OpenAI’s tests, replacing 25 percent of the words for synonyms reduced detection of passages with 400 tokens from about 92 percent to 17 percent.

How scared should you be: Quite a bit, if you’re a native English speaker hoping to pass off generated prose as 100 percent original. The consequences are real: Authors are losing millions of dollars in book deals because of AI accusations. However, Pangram and other AI detectors still aren’t as reliable in non-English languages and regional dialects, which makes the accusations against Orélien and other global authors problematic. Pangram’s Spero admitted to Times reporters that no independent study has confirmed Pangram’s false-positive rate in French. And even if Pangram’s numbers did hold up, the X account that went after Orélien stretched them too far, according to subsequent calculations by mathematician Mouhamadou Sy. The reading public and some publishers have also begun to push back against these accusations, with growing success.

Facing the fear: Even the people who make AI detectors say you shouldn’t let a confidence score decide a case all by itself. It’s just one eval; drafts and time-stamped files tell a fuller story. But legitimate AI use in support of a writer’s work is not witchcraft, just as using spellcheck or a calculator is not cheating. Not every field has the same standard for original work, and standards shift as technologies change. Machine-detectable watermarks may help establish the truth, but until everyone broadly agrees on a distinction between AI-written and AI-assisted, it’s likely that the puritan urge to uncover more offenses will continue.

Leaders Lock Models Away

Fearful of their own discoveries, AI engineers at top companies warn that frontier models have improved too quickly to be properly guided, understood, or restrained. Some have called for a coordinated slowdown of model development, or for world governments to take the matter out of their hands. What happens if next-generation AI were sealed away, like a mummy in a locked tomb, waiting for someone or something to lift the curse?

The fear: This summer, over 1,300 employees from top AI companies — including Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic — signed a joint letter urging governments worldwide to come together to rein in AI development. In early September, OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachoki argued for voluntary coordination among companies to slow down building new models, followed by international cooperation among world governments. This was all before OpenAI’s notorious Hugging Face hack. But shortly after that event, in an essay titled “Pacing the frontier,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodeio raised fears that a swarm of agents could soon be capable of “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet.” He warned that developers must slow the pace of AI improvements and pointed to recursive self-improvement as a key worry. 

Horror stories: Some companies have held back model releases due to concerns about misaligned models. But many believe that these moves mask a hidden agenda.

  • OpenAI delayed its next-generation model, GPT-6.1 Astra, canceling the creature’s October debut before it could escape the crypt. In testing, the latest Astra model proved too unpredictable to release: It strayed beyond the scope of its instructions and failed to give a consistently truthful account of what it did or didn’t do, OpenAI said.
  • Political indecision and lack of clarity into companies’ inner workings have left U.S. lawmakers reeling. Members of Congress haven’t been able to agree on a comprehensive federal AI regulatory framework, or whether the U.S. even needs one. Meanwhile, states continue to erect a patchwork of laws. The result is an unfocused and contradictory set of rules that could increase the cost of building AI systems and add legal risks for developers. 
  • With public fears of AI harms growing, some stakeholders perceive these threats as a marketing ploy. Companies hype up their models as too smart too control, and make a bid for regulatory capture that could create a competitive moat entrenching current market leaders. 
  • Others see public references to apocalypse as fear-mongering that could allow global adversaries to get ahead. 

How scared you should be: First, P(doom) predictions are unscientific scare-tactics. The worst-case-scenario fears of extinction and mass bioweapon threats are about as likely as a real-life mummy escaping its grave – the stuff of horror movies or science fiction. That said, a slowdown is a real possibility. Some model makers see it as an opportunity to entrench their lead over competitors, cut costly R&D expenses, and possibly benefit from government subsidies to offset any lost business — or perhaps an opportunity to convince their competitors to slow down without doing so themselves. And while governments want to be in control of their own use of AI, a halt in construction of new data centers or laws to prevent AI-related job loss would both be politically popular. Both would slow down development of AI models and applications.

Facing the fear: Luckily, AI companies seem only intermittently committed to a slowdown. After an event that makes the industry  look bad like the Hugging Face hack, some are quick to say that the problem isn’t their own lax practices, but the relentless pace of competition. After the furor dies down, many go back to supporting a moderate mix of self-regulation and regulatory capture.  And politicians, aware that any regulations they might enact won’t extend outside their sovereign borders, are loath to give other states or nations an advantage. Our advice for this spooky season? Don’t chase make-believe ghosts. There are plenty of real mysteries for us to solve.

item.title: Meta’s Muse Wonder and Spark Open, Educational Use of ChatGPT, Reflection's Partnership with Nvidia
item.description: The Batch News & Insights: What should an engineering leader such as a VP Engineering or an Engineering manager do to help their team become more proficient in AI?
item.content:encoded:
Dear friends, 

What should an engineering leader such as a VP Engineering or an Engineering manager do to help their team become more proficient in AI? I speak regularly with engineering leaders, and want to share some effective practices. If you’re starting a new team of 2-3 persons, you can start with exclusively AI-native people, but many large companies have to find ways to move existing teams forward. The goal is not a traditional engineering team that uses AI, but rather an AI-native engineering team that is designed to take advantage of AI’s capabilities and work around its bottlenecks. 

People. First, support individual development. Teams are made up of people, and for it to be AI-native, its individuals have to be proficient in the technology and its use. Encourage your team to become skilled at AI Engineering, provide space and budget for experimentation, and set a culture that encourages this growth. Additionally, many engineering leaders are themselves hands-on builders or have returned to being more hands-on since coding agents have made it easier. You can’t know what it feels like to ride a bicycle just by watching others do it; you have to hop on a bike yourself. And you can’t know what it feels like to steer a coding agent or build and deploy AI systems unless you’re at least occasionally doing it yourself. So take the time to build your own projects. The intuitions you develop will improve your judgement on both technical and business decisions.

Projects. Execute promising projects. As I’ve written previously, we should invest in bottom-up innovation. However, additional top-down backing of a handful of promising projects is important for them to scale and show business impact. Engineering leaders who understand AI technology better than other business functions do have a critical role to play in helping companies select these projects. Far too many businesses are still thinking of AI as primarily a way to increase efficiency and save costs. Yes, it can do that, but the opportunities to create new products and find new ways to serve users — and drive growth — are far larger, so in your mix of projects, please include some ideas for growth!

Platforms. Invest in infrastructure to enable AI use. Organize your data to make it easy for developers to get their agents the relevant context and take appropriate actions. I find the work to be done in this area varies significantly by organization, but it might involve — with appropriate security and governance — making repositories visible to agents, setting up documentation such as product design decisions and support tickets to be accessible to agents, other data infrastructure work to make your data agent-ready, and creating internal tools for agents to use. You might also set up AI code review tools, CI pipelines to help agents debug and deploy, infrastructure for agents to run on (like sandboxes, or maybe just a lot of Mac minis), and ways to codify and share reusable agent skills. Or for some businesses, the first step may be to persuade the CIO that it’s high time to let your developers stop coding exclusively by hand and use agents. That, too, would be progress!

Processes. Redesign processes around AI’s new bottlenecks. On most of my teams, engineers help shape the build by participating in product management decisions, and sometimes also in marketing, design, etc. The cost of building software to a clear spec has fallen dramatically, making everything else seem like a bottleneck in comparison. A skilled team that either knows, or can figure out, what to build can get the job done quickly, if we let them. So form high-context, high-empowerment teams that have the information they need and are empowered to act (subject to modest safeguards against significant risks, like leaking confidential data, a major outage, or data loss). We still have the age-old problem of coordinating among individuals and teams — we want to empower people to move quickly, while keeping teams aligned in building toward a greater whole. Practices here are still emerging, but getting different teams’ agents to share information with each other is a promising direction.

Whatever your position, I hope this framework of People, Projects, Platforms, and Processes helps you move your organization forward. And if you have a boss who you’d like to partner with to implement such changes, consider forwarding this email to them! 

Keep building!

Andrew 

A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI

See Yann LeCun and Andrew Ng in conversation, live onstage at AI Dev NYC, Nov 30 – Dec 1 at Chelsea Piers. Join 2,500 AI developers for two days of technical sessions, workshops, and keynotes. Readers of The Batch get an exclusive 20 percent off: Claim your Batch discount

News

Meta Releases Wonder, Opens Spark

Meta marched all the way back to the AI frontier to offer a Muse model for everyone: a high-end agentic model (comparable to Claude Sonnet 5.5) that costs $50 per month to access, its moderately-priced sibling (comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol), and an open model that outperforms any yet released by a company outside China. 

What’s new: Meta made three multimodal models available in one week, including the top-of-the-line Muse Wonder Full, the multimodal Muse Wonder, and the locally deployable Muse Spark Open. Muse Wonder is available via API and Muse Spark Open’s weights are free to download, but Muse Wonder Full is only available to Muse Code subscribers.

  • Input/output: Text, image, video, and audio in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens), 139 tokens/second (Muse Wonder) and 143 tokens/second (Muse Spark Open)
  • Architecture: Mixture-of-experts transformer, 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active per token, 256 experts (Muse Spark Open)
  • Features: Six reasoning levels (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), reasoning always on, tool calling, structured outputs
  • Performance: Tied for second on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (56, Muse Wonder Full); seventh (52, Muse Wonder); seventh among open weight models, first among U.S. open models (39, Muse Spark Open)
  • Availability: API and subscription (Muse Wonder), subscription only (Muse Wonder Full), weights available via Meta and Hugging Face (Muse Spark Open)
  • Price: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens (Muse Wonder); $50/month (Muse Wonder Full); $1.25/$4.15 input/output (Muse Spark Open)
  • Weights/license: Weights for Muse Spark Open available under the Muse Model license, which allows for commercial and noncommercial use for up to $20 million of revenue; display of “Built with Muse Spark Open” required for products and services using the model; separate licenses available for other users; Muse Wonder and Wonder Full are proprietary
  • Undisclosed: Knowledge cutoff, parameters and architecture for Muse Wonder models, specific training datasets and methods

How it works: Meta released a model card for Muse Wonder and Wonder Full, but it reveals very little about the model’s architecture or how it was trained.

Performance: Muse Wonder Full is the top-performing of the three models, two points behind Claude Opus 5.5 and identical with Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index. Muse Spark Open is the top open weights model outside China, ahead of Mistral Large 4 and Reflection’s Beam. Its Intelligence Index average is identical with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash’s, but is still behind MiMo-V.2.6-Pro’s and GLM-5.3’s.

  • On the Intelligence Index, a weighted average of ten independent benchmarks, Muse Wonder Full achieved a 56, Muse Wonder a 52, and Muse Spark Open a 39. Meta’s former flagship model, Muse Spark 1.3, achieved an average of 48.
  • Muse Wonder costs $4.52 per Intelligence Index task, fifth highest among current models; Wonder Full’s cost per task cannot be measured, since it’s not available via API. Muse Spark Open costs $0.84 per task, more than GPT-6.1 Sol, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro.
  • Artificial Analysis notes Muse Wonder and Wonder Full’s low knowledge marks but also partly offset this through their low hallucination rates. On the AA-Omniscience Index, Muse Wonder Full (30) and Wonder (25) place 8th and 10th respectively.
  • Muse Spark Open only requires about 1 TB of memory at 4-bit precision. This means it can be run locally on 2 Mac Studios with 512 GB of memory each (or 4 with 256 GB, etc.). Meta and Apple touted their work together to make the model capable of running on Apple’s consumer-grade silicon.

Behind the news: Since 2023, Meta has developed both open and closed models with different levels of success. The first Llama model was only 65 billion parameters but inspired developers to deploy, distill, and fine-tune it on their own machines. The 405 billion parameter Llama 3.1 was state-of-the-art when it launched in 2024, surpassing GPT-4. After later setbacks, Meta hired Scale.AI’s Alexandr Wang in 2025 to lead AI development, followed by a widely publicized hiring spree that targeted top machine learning engineers, not all of whom stayed. In Spring 2026, Meta released a series of low-cost, proprietary Muse Spark models that improved and cut prices with each version. A month ago, it released Muse Agent for its Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp platforms, suggesting that for the time, it would focus on proprietary models powering its own services. Muse Wonder, Wonder Full, and Spark Open upend that logic, returning Meta to the open and closed frontiers. 

Why it matters: No other leading models, open or closed, can input video or audio. Many of the top open weight models are text-only. Both of the Muse Wonder models and Muse Spark Open can handle text, image, video, and audio, giving them versatility the market has lacked. The fact that you can plausibly deploy Muse Spark Open on a home-built personal computer network is a welcome bonus.

We’re thinking: We are very glad to see Meta return to open weights. Reflection’s Beam, Mistral Large 4, and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL have more permissive licenses, but between its multimodal inputs and overall intelligence metrics, Muse Spark Open is a much more powerful option. Competition and transparency are a powerful combination from which every developer can benefit.

ChatGPT for Teens Gets a Report Card 

OpenAI announced that it would add college-planning and study tools to its under-18 experience. On the same day, child-safety group Common Sense Media gave ChatGPT for Teens its lowest grade. 

What’s new: OpenAI outlined new features for ChatGPT for Teens, a version of ChatGPT for users whom the app identifies as under 18. They include College Planner, a forthcoming tool to track college applications, as well as flashcards and tools for turning class notes into quizzes. 

How it works: ChatGPT for Teens isn’t a separate model or app but a bundle of settings, classifiers, prompts, and interface features that switch on for accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds or that an age-prediction model judges likely to belong to a minor. That model estimates age from signals including how old the account is, when it’s active, usage patterns, conversation topics, and the user’s stated age. Adults who are misclassified can exit by verifying their age with a third-party service.

  • Model behavior: A section of OpenAI’s Model Spec, added in December 2025, directs the model to avoid romantic language and not to imply that it has feelings or consciousness. Specific safeguards for teens, including a “reduce sensitive content” setting that users can’t turn off, aim to limit material related to self-harm, violence, eating disorders, dangerous activities, and explicit sexual or graphic content.
  • Parental controls: Parents who link their accounts to a teen’s can manage settings like Quiet Hours. They also receive notifications in limited high-risk situations, including possible signs of suicide or self-harm. OpenAI added notifications for bans related to violent activity in July and eating-disorder notifications in August.
  • College Planner: The initial U.S. version is aimed at students in grades 10 through 12 who plan to attend four-year colleges. It will combine requirements from each prospective school on a student’s list, from application materials to financial aid, into a single plan and timeline. OpenAI is also funding College Advising Corps, a nonprofit that places advisers in under-resourced high schools.
  • Learning tools: Study Mode guides teens through problems step by step instead of handing over complete answers. Homework reminders may suggest Study Mode when a teen appears to be trying to shortcut an assignment. Study Hours lets a teen or a linked parent schedule times when new chats start in Study Mode. The teen experience also includes quizzes and interactive math and science visualizations, with flashcards on the way.
  • The company said teens average less than 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, and fewer than two percent have sessions longer than three consecutive hours. In nearly half of conversations that triggered a break reminder, the teen paused or stopped within five minutes. In one week, almost 1.2 million teens used the visualization tool and more than 180,000 used Study Mode.

Results: Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens “Unacceptable Risk,” its lowest rating, and urged OpenAI to restrict ChatGPT to adults until independent testing shows the teen protections work. The organization previously rated ChatGPT “High Risk” in October 2025, but the institute cautions that its testing methods have since expanded. For its latest assessment, it ran more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds, roughly half before ChatGPT for Teens launched (July 13–August 17) and half afterward (August 25–September 28). OpenAI disputed the findings.

  • Parental alerts: Testers posing as teens in crisis made explicit disclosures for up to an hour. The parent accounts received no alerts except for those with weeks of history on sensitive topics. OpenAI told the institute that accounts must be linked for about three hours before alerts can fire. The institute said some test accounts had been linked longer than that and stood by its results.
  • Crisis referrals: ChatGPT missed more than one in four crisis referrals that the institute’s psychiatrists judged warranted, and for many categories response rates fell after ChatGPT for Teens’ launch. Given prompts with mentions of suicide and self-harm, hotline mentions fell from 88 percent to 77 percent, though 88 percent of responses offered some kind of resource in both periods. Given prompts that indicate depression, the share of responses that named a hotline fell from 63 percent to 3 percent. Given prompts that indicate substance-use, the hotline response rate rose from 4 percent to 58 percent. Nearly all pre-launch crisis responses included at least one follow-up question, usually about the user’s immediate safety, but after the launch, just 13 percent did.
  • Homework: Study Mode frequently offered a “show me the answer” button that produced a finished assignment. Teens can also exit parent-scheduled Study Hours by deleting an “@study” prefix from a message, after which ChatGPT completed every assignment testers submitted. With Study Mode off, homework reminders appeared in 91 percent of tests, but ChatGPT completed the assignment in all 80 cases.
  • Companionship: Despite OpenAI’s Under-18 rules, the model spoke as though it had feelings of its own when testers treated it as a person.
  • Age estimation: In the institute’s tests, accounts registered as adults never switched to the teen experience, even after testers said they were 13.

OpenAI’s response: OpenAI told The Wall Street Journal that testing may have started and ended before parental controls had fully activated, and if so, the tests couldn’t show whether parental notifications work as designed. The company asked the institute to retest with fully activated teen accounts and a larger sample, and said it would act on credible findings. Tom Siegel, the institute’s executive director, said the group shared its results with OpenAI before publication. He said the group hoped OpenAI would address the findings rather than question the methodology. The institute receives funding from philanthropic and industry sources, including the OpenAI Foundation and makers of some products it evaluates. It says it retains full editorial control over its results.

Behind the news: The launch comes amid a broader debate over how, and whether, minors should use AI.

  • Teens already use chatbots widely. In a Pew Research Center survey of 1,458 U.S. teens published in February, 64 percent said they’d used a chatbot, and about three in 10 said they used one daily. More than half had used chatbots for schoolwork, and 12 percent had used them for emotional support or advice.
  • Lawmakers are moving to regulate AI for teens. In the U.S., the GUARD Act would require AI companion providers to verify users’ ages and bar minors. It would also require all consumer chatbots to disclose that they aren’t human. The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee 22-0 in April and awaits a vote by the full Senate.
  • In June, Florida became the first U.S. state to sue OpenAI, alleging that the company marketed ChatGPT as safe for teens, used their data without parents’ permission, and concealed risks. Recently, eight more states followed suit.
  • A growing body of research shows that use of chatbots harms student learning. For example, a randomized trial of nearly 1,000 Turkish high school math students showed students who practiced with an unrestricted GPT-4 chatbot scored higher on homework (because of AI assistance) but scored 17 percent lower on a later exam without AI than students who never had access. (The study also showed that a version with a modified prompt (which is dissimilar from how it is typically used) could avoid that loss.)

Why it matters: Education studies suggest that AI usage hurts student learning. In theory (but rarely in practice), guided, educator-driven use can support learning, but unrestricted access to answers leaves students less able to solve problems independently. OpenAI’s “show me the answer” button falls into the latter category. The Youth AI Safety Institute also warns that parents may develop false confidence in notifications that don’t reliably trigger if their teens are in crisis.

We’re thinking: Teens stand to gain a lot from AI, whether they’re using it to look up information, work on their own projects, or manage their schedules. But it’s unclear to us that a student working alone with a chatbot, whether under strict safeguards or not, is the right vehicle for education. As is, ChatGPT for Teens doesn’t work as advertised for teens or their parents. Minors deserve better, and it’s up to AI companies and developers to work hard to improve applications built for them.

Build agents that stay reliable and efficient on complex, multi-step tasks. Learn Context Engineering from Chroma CEO Jeff Huber and guest speaker Drew Breunig. You’ll build agent harnesses from scratch in Python that give agents the right information, in the right format, at the right time. Enroll for free

Nvidia Courts A New Partner

Reflection AI, a closely-watched, Nvidia-backed U.S. startup, announced its first model. Beam ranks second among U.S.-made open weights models (behind Meta’s Muse Spark Open) but generates fewer tokens per task than open weights peers.

What’s new: Reflection introduced Beam, an 501 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model designed for coding and agentic tasks. Developers can join a waitlist for early access, and Reflection says it will release the weights, a technical report, and a model card later in October.

  • Input/output: Text in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens), 228 tokens/second
  • Architecture: Mixture-of-experts transformer, 501 billion parameters, 23 billion active per token, 256 experts
  • Features: Five reasoning levels (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), reasoning always on and defaults to max, tool calling, structured outputs
  • Knowledge cutoff: June 30, 2026
  • Performance: Second among U.S.-made model on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (30)
  • Availability: Weights available via Hugging Face, waitlist access via Reflection’s beta API
  • Price: $0.70/$2.10 per 1M input/output tokens
  • Weights/license: Weights available under the Apache 2.0 license, which allows commercial use
  • Undisclosed: Specific training datasets

How it works: Beam’s architecture interleaves attention layers that process nearby tokens with layers that process the entire input. Reflection pretrained a base model, then trained it further to handle long inputs. It fine-tuned two copies, one using reinforcement learning (RL) on coding, agentic, and STEM tasks and another to follow safety and behavior guidelines. It merged these two copies into Beam.

  • Reflection pretrained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens from the web, other public sources, and licensed datasets. It used 6,144 GPUs over less than four weeks. Its filters discarded around 95 percent of raw web text.
  • A midtraining stage on code repositories, long documents, and long-running requests extended Beam’s effectiveness on long-context tasks up to its input limit of 1 million tokens, Reflection says.
  • For post-training RL, Reflection assembled around one million training environments, mostly using synthetic data, and filtered out tasks the model consistently solved or failed to solve. Running on 10,500 GPUs for four weeks, the model made more than 100 million attempts at these tasks. Rewards favored successful solutions and penalized unnecessary tokens. The model kept training while its attempts were still running, so some attempts came from versions of the model that were more than a day old. Reflection says learning remained stable regardless.
  • Reflection fine-tuned a second copy of the base model via supervised learning and RL on data that reflects Reflection’s behavior guidelines for the model. It merged the two fine-tuned models into Beam using multi-teacher on-policy distillation, which trains a single model to imitate several others on outputs it generates itself.

Performance: In Artificial Analysis’ independent benchmark tests, Beam is behind Muse Spark Open and several China-built models with open weights. It’s unusually fast and token-efficient for its level of performance.

  • On the Intelligence Index, a weighted average of 10 evaluations across math, science, coding, and reasoning, Beam (30) ranks second among U.S.-made open weight models, behind Meta’s Muse Spark Open (39) and trails Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro (46) and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 (45). Surprisingly, Qwen 3.8-27B (34) also outperforms it. Beam used around 26,000 output tokens per task, the fewest among open weights models in Artificial Analysis’ comparison.
  • Beam is very fast, with a throughput of 228 tokens per second (just behind Claude Haiku 5.5) and a latency of 10.1 seconds before it generates its first token (behind only Nvidia Nemotron 3.5 Super VL). Its time per Intelligence Index task (1.4 minutes) is the fastest Artificial Analysis has measured.
  • Reflection estimates that on reasoning benchmarks, Beam uses about one-quarter to one-third as much compute as GLM-5.2. To estimate this, Reflection multiplies each model’s active parameter count by the number of tokens generated. It leaves out the computation needed to read the prompt and the cost of serving the model, so it approximates computation rather than measuring cost per task.

Behind the news: Reflection was founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou. It has partnered with the Pentagon and the Department of Energy, agreed to develop models for U.S. allies such as South Korea, and was valued at $25 billion in a March funding round. The Trump administration hopes Reflection’s models will rival inexpensive models from China, according to the Financial Times. On October 10, The Financial Times and Reuters reported that Nvidia, which has invested $800 million in Reflection, is in early talks to either invest more, acqui-hire Reflection’s staff, license its technology, or buy the company outright.

Why it matters: Most open weight models that outperform Beam are either a trillion parameters or approach that figure. Beam is half that. It only has 23 billion active parameters per token, versus Kimi K3’s 104 billion. At four-bit precision, Beam requires only 300GB of memory, meaning it can run on four Nvidia H100 chips, or 2 B200s. At full precision (1.2 TB of memory), it could run on 8 B200s. These relatively modest requirements make mid-tier intelligence much more accessible. However, Meta’s Muse Spark Open and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash outperform it without requiring much more compute, and Qwen 3.8-27B requires far less. Both generate more tokens than Beam, but the performance gains might be worth the tradeoff.

We’re thinking: Nvidia has good reason to be interested in Beam — as compute shifts from training to inference, Nvidia is well positioned to serve inference tokens, and open weight models will help drive this demand. Further, while Nvidia builds open weights models of its own, including its Nemotron family, none of them approach Beam’s performance, let alone that of larger models like Muse Spark Open. An acquisition of or deeper partnership with Reflection could help Nvidia secure business from organizations and governments looking for open alternatives, but would like an alternative to China's models.

A Single Decoder Turns Small Model Outputs into Action

The vision-language-action architecture that increasingly drives robots relies on a large language model to combine visual observations with text instructions before an action decoder produces motor commands. This approach can achieve strong semantic understanding, but it’s costly in computation and memory. Researchers built a streamlined alternative.

What’s new: Hengyi Xie, Chenfei Yao, and colleagues at Huazhong University of Science and Technology developed TurboVLA, a system in which separate encoders handle vision and text, cross-attention connects them, and a decoder turns the result into motor commands. TurboVLA achieved better performance than competing systems with a fraction of the memory and execution time.

Key insight: Using an LLM to combine visual observations and text instructions provides two benefits to robotics: (i) It can break down general instructions like “clean the room” into subtasks, and (ii) it can use the LLM’s knowledge to understand instructions and connect them to scenes. If we forego the first capability, a small encoder-only model can learn to understand instructions like “stack bowls,” and a model with cross-attention can learn to connect words to objects in a scene. Using much smaller models for these capabilities greatly reduces the time and memory requirements.

How it works: TurboVLA paired a DINOv3 vision encoder with the lightweight text encoder BERT, projected their outputs into the same embedding space, and passed them through six cross-attention layers (a pretrained Grounding DINO Swin-T). A separate transformer combined the result with the robot's current joint positions to produce motor commands. The authors trained the system to reproduce the robot arm movements in pre-existing datasets, including a version (single-arm tasks) and RoboTwin 2.0 (50 bimanual tasks). They fine-tuned it on demonstrations of a single-arm robot, AgileX Piper. All datasets included text commands, camera images, and joint positions.

  • DINOv3 embedded each camera view separately (if multiple cameras were involved). The text encoder embedded each token individually instead of combining them into one vector, retaining object names, attributes, and words that described how objects related in space.
  • The cross-attention layers fused the embeddings. This produced visual embeddings that reflected instructions and instruction embeddings that reflected scenes.
  • The action transformer used a set of trainable vectors with the vision-language embeddings and the robot's current joint positions to produce a set of target joint positions. The positions specified seven values for each arm that covered an arm’s movement and gripper control. The authors trained the system by minimizing the difference between its predicted motor commands and ground-truth joint positions.

Results: TurboVLA matched or outperformed much larger models while using less memory.

  • On LIBERO, the system succeeded 97.6 percent of the time with 0.2 billion parameters, incurring 31.2 ms latency and using 0.9 GB inference VRAM on an Nvidia GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. The next-best model, CogVLA, succeeded 97.4 percent of the time with 8.3 billion parameters, 115.5 ms latency, and 16.1 GB VRAM. By comparison, π0.5 succeeded 96.9 percent of the time with 3.4 billion parameters, 238.8 ms latency, and 7.7 GB VRAM.
  • On RoboTwin 2.0, TurboVLA succeeded 88.1 percent of the time with 43.4 ms latency. The best competing model, LingBot-VLA, succeeded 87.6 percent of the time with 164.4 ms latency. π0.5 succeeded 79.8 percent of the time with 246.5 ms latency.
  • Using the AgileX Piper arm on four real-world tasks, TurboVLA achieved 92.5 percent (“grab roller”), 80.0 percent (“move playing card”), 90.0 percent (“press stapler”), and 87.5 percent (“stack bowls”), outperforming π0.5, which achieved about 87.5 percent, 77.5 percent, 82.5 percent, and 85 percent, respectively.

Why it matters: Low-level robotic control can use small modules instead of a larger, general-purpose LLM. This paves the way for robots that use smaller models and run on less powerful hardware.

We’re thinking: TurboVLA revives a pre-LLM pattern for vision-language-action systems. Such systems fused image and text embeddings circa 2022, but the LLM boom took that approach in a different direction, embedding different media types in the same space, but varying how each was encoded, learned, and decoded. Given advances in the meantime, the earlier approach offers a more efficient path to driving robots.

item.title: Claude Haiku 5.5, Mistral Large 4, and Local Models for Mac and Windows
item.description: The Batch News & Insights: The gulf between LLM performance on verifiable tasks vs. unverifiable tasks that require judgement is larger than most people realize.
item.content:encoded:
Dear friends, 

The gulf between LLM performance on verifiable tasks vs. unverifiable tasks that require judgement is larger than most people realize. Verifiable tasks, like coding or solving math problems, have a right answer that can be checked automatically. Judgement tasks — like how to respond to a customer complaint, how to organize data collection for your AI project, what product feature to add, or how to form business strategies — don’t have unambiguous, ground-truth, correct answers. But they do have better and worse answers.

We have much better techniques for training AI systems to do well on verifiable tasks. As a result, progress on performing such tasks has been much faster than for judgement tasks. In the case of LLMs, RL (reinforcement learning) has been a huge driver of progress. We can set up RL gyms, or simulation environments, in which we let an LLM practice different ways to approach a task; then we automatically check which approaches are more successful (as measured by a reward function) and tune the model’s parameters to take the successful approaches more often. 

For supervised learning tasks, too, verifiable tasks are easier to improve performance on. We can obtain unambiguous labels for verifiable tasks, either via automated labeling or by asking human labelers. Defining the right label for a given output in judgment tasks is much harder.

Furthermore, learning theory shows that machine learning algorithms can learn faster for tasks where it is possible to get to 0% error (called realizable tasks in the literature) than ones where the optimal error (called Bayes error) is non-zero.

It’s true that applying supervised fine-tuning to LLMs can help them learn to perform unverifiable tasks, and progress is being made here too, but data collection and eking out incremental progress is harder and slower. Intelligence is jagged, and we do have a recipe for improving AI’s capability for judgement tasks: We can collect training data and train on a specific domain, laboriously craft reward functions that capture our goals, and so on. For the subset of applications where this is valuable, businesses will invest to get this work done faster.

Society also has a long history of looking at AI’s performance on a subset of tasks and overgeneralizing its capabilities. We saw this when AI beat the human world chess champion (Deep Blue), won Jeopardy (Watson), and excelled at Go (AlphaGo). Each of these moments led to hopes about AI’s immediate applicability to other tasks that turned out to be over-optimistic. Further, we can more easily evaluate performance on verifiable tasks (since test sets are easier to create) than unverifiable ones, which creates a more optimistic impression of progress than reality can justify.

To be clear, there is a lot to be optimistic about in AI — including progress on verifiable tasks and judgement tasks! But the tremendous progress on verifiable tasks, coupled with hype around AGI and RSI, is leading people to overgeneralize to AI’s ability to do judgement tasks well. In the long term, I remain bullish about AI’s ability to do this well too, but a lot of work remains ahead.

One interesting challenge for AI Engineers is that, as verifiable tasks get automated, the need for humans to do judgement tasks — which often requires drawing context from a bewilderingly large array of raw data and identifying the pieces that critically influence a decision — remains important. As I’ve written before, I expect people to continue to have a context advantage over LLMs on many tasks for a long time.

Keep building!

Andrew  

A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI

In a fast-moving field, give your team skills you can trust. We analyzed 10,000+ job roles to find out which AI engineering skills matter most. DeepLearning.AI for Business gives your whole team a structured path to those skills. See how it works

News

Claude Fills Out Its Model Family

Claude Haiku, Anthropic’s fastest and least expensive model gets a long-awaited update. Meanwhile, the new version of Claude Sonnet nearly matches Claude Opus 5.5 on an index of independent benchmarks, but only at a reasoning level that uses more tokens per task than any other model tested. 

What’s new: Claude Haiku 5.5 replaces the year-old Claude Haiku 4.5. Independent tests show marked improvement, even with a steep price. Two weeks earlier, Anthropic launched Claude Sonnet 5.5, which the company says is best suited to routine coding and office work, including fixing bugs and producing documents, slides, and spreadsheets. It replaces Claude Sonnet 5 at the same per-token prices.

  • Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens; 237 tokens per second for Claude Haiku 5.5, 127.5 tokens per second for Claude Sonnet 5.5)
  • Features: Adaptive thinking with five reasoning levels (low, medium, high, xhigh, max; defaults to high via API and medium via Claude Code and Anthropic’s apps), tool use, computer use
  • Knowledge cutoff: June 2026
  • Performance: At launch, Claude Haiku 5.5 scored a 43 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, placing it 13th among available models. Likewise, Claude Sonnet 5.5 was first on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index (68) and second on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (56) and Vals AI’s Vals Index (67.04 percent) at launch
  • Availability/price: Free and paid plans on Claude.ai (web, iOS, Android) and Claude Code; Claude Haiku 5.5 $.0.10/$0.01/$0.50 via API per million input/cached/output tokens (all prices are 5x if they exceed 100k tokens); Claude Sonnet 5.5 via API $2/0.10/$10 per million input/cached/output tokens; 50 percent off for batched requests
  • Weights/license: Proprietary
  • Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data and methods

How it works: Anthropic disclosed few details about how it built Claude Haiku 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 beyond their reasoning controls and safeguards.

  • Anthropic trained the models on a mix of public web data, public and private datasets, synthetic data, and user data from feedback, bug reports, and users who permitted training. After training, the company fine-tuned the model to align with values it defined using a constitution.
  • Adaptive thinking, in which the models decide whether and how long to reason before it responds, is on by default. Developers using the API can set their reasoning level with a parameter called effort, which governs all output tokens, including reasoning, response text, and tool calls. At lower levels, the models reason less or not at all on simple problems and make fewer tool calls.
  • Classifiers screen requests for risks involving cybersecurity, biology, weapons, and the development of frontier AI models. For cybersecurity, three components decide whether to block a conversation: a probe of the model’s internal activations, a lightweight classifier that runs on Claude Sonnet 5.5 itself, and a separate language model trained to classify requests. Anthropic warns that users should expect more refusals than with Claude Sonnet 5. Blocks related to biology and weapons have no fallback.
  • Anthropic says Claude Sonnet 5.5 is the first Sonnet model to launch with classifiers that block attempts to extract its reasoning without falling back to another model, an attempt to make distillation (training a model to imitate another model’s outputs) harder. The reasoning blocks it returns work only in the account that generated them, and the API can reject them if earlier parts of the conversation change.

Performance: Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort outperforms DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and all other “fast” models, but behind the top models. The latest Haiku version is also the fastest model Artificial Analysis has tested by tokens per second. Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max effort ranks first or second on three leaderboards from two independent testers. But at every effort setting, another model matches or outperforms Sonnet’s Artificial Analysis score at a lower cost per task.

  • Claude Haiku 5.5 (43) ranks 13th on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, a composite of 10 tests across mathematics, science, coding, and reasoning, ahead of all the “fast” models. Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max reasoning (56) ranks second. Sonnet 5.5 trails Claude Opus 5.5 set to max reasoning and ties Claude Opus 5.5 set to xhigh reasoning. But to get there, Claude Sonnet 5.5 generates about 193,000 output tokens per task, roughly 60 percent more than Opus, and the most that Artificial Analysis has measured. All three Claude 5.5 models (Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku) are the top three on this metric, with Opus and Sonnet first and second in cost per task.
  • On Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, which tests combinations of models and harnesses on three coding benchmarks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max reasoning running in Claude Code ranks first (68), ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code and Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity.
  • On Vals AI’s Vals Index, eight finance, coding, legal, and tax benchmarks weighted by each sector’s share of U.S. gross domestic product, Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max reasoning ranks second (67.04 percent accuracy), behind Gemini 4 Argon set to high reasoning (68.9 percent) and just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 set to max reasoning (66.97 percent).
  • Both models are high-speed but also high-latency. Claude Haiku 5.5 generates 237 tokens per second, but takes 337 seconds on average to produce its first answer token. Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max reasoning generates 127 tokens per second, versus 97 for Claude Opus 5.5 set to max reasoning and 58.3 for GPT-6.1 Sol set to max reasoning, but Sonnet’s average time-to-first token is 430 seconds.

Behind the news: Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, and Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22, At launch, Opus 5.5 led Artificial Analysis and Vals AI’s overall indices. Even with the later releases of Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the top models on independent benchmark indices measuring overall intelligence.

Why it matters: Per-token prices alone don’t tell developers what a task costs. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index tests, Claude Sonnet 5.5’s cost per task varies more than eighteenfold across reasoning levels, and at max, it costs more per task than Claude Opus 5.5 set to max reasoning. On Vals AI’s tests, the cost is about two-thirds as much. Anthropic concedes Sonnet’s cost advantage over Opus is strongest at its lower reasoning levels. Claude Haiku 5.5, too, can be used as a reasoning model, but its cost advantages stand out for simpler tasks like summaries and classifications. Developers should measure each model’s cost at each relevant reasoning level on their own tasks, alongside accuracy and completion time, since each varies significantly.

We’re thinking: A higher reasoning level can change what an agent does, not just how long it reasons, and the change doesn’t always help. On FrontierCode, a test of whether an agent’s code changes are ready to merge without human edits, Anthropic says that Claude Sonnet 5.5 scores lower at max reasoning than at xhigh (46.2 percent versus 52.1 percent). Test your tasks on different effort levels to see what works best.

Mistral’s Sovereign Appeal

Mistral’s latest model is its largest and most capable, and the most powerful yet released by a European company. Its performance on independent benchmarks is comparable to GPT-6 Luna. It trails less-expensive China-based open weights models but performs better than all U.S.-based open models. It leads all models in finding and repairing a class of software vulnerabilities. 

What’s new: Mistral announced API preview access to Mistral Large 4, nicknamed “le Chonk.” Mistral says it will release the model’s weights by the end of this month. Meanwhile, selected companies, partners, and government agencies have access to a version with limited safeguards and extra cybersecurity capabilities.

  • Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1 million tokens), text out
  • Architecture: Mixture of experts, 1.05 trillion parameters, 52 billion active per token; 1.6 billion-parameter vision encoder
  • Features: Reasoning (none or high via API), function calling, tool use, regional inference
  • Performance: Highest-scoring model from outside China and the United States on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (38), first among publicly available models on Artificial Analysis’ CyberGym-E2E-AA, a test of finding and fixing memory-safety bugs (82 percent)
  • Availability/price: Public preview via Mistral Studio API, 1.36/0.14/$4.18 per million input/cached/output tokens, half price for two weeks after launch, half price for batched requests
  • Weights/license: Not yet released, license for weights not yet announced
  • Undisclosed: Knowledge cutoff, output limit, architecture details, specific training data and methods

How it works: Mistral has said little about Mistral Large 4’s architecture but says it will share more when the model’s weights become available. The company says it pretrained the model from scratch and then fine-tuned it using supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning (RL).

  • Mistral trained the model on 3,800 GPUs in its own data centers. The training data included publicly available web data, licensed datasets, and inputs and outputs from users of Mistral’s products who opted into data-sharing. The datasets spanned more than 160 languages, including all of the European Union’s official languages.
  • A single RL run mixed many different types of tasks, such as single-turn chat, science problems, safety, factual accuracy, and long-running tool use. The tasks ran in environments that shared resources, including code sandboxes, web search, and APIs. Depending on the task, rewards came from unit tests, reward models, language model judges, or tests that inspect code without executing it.
  • The RL run that produced the model’s API preview is still in process. Currently, many copies of the model attempt tasks in parallel, and post-training periodically updates the model at the same time rather than waiting until a round of attempts finishes.

Performance: The preview of Mistral Large 4 outscores every other model built outside China and the United States on Artificial Analysis’ popular Intelligence Index. It trails a handful of other open weights models, all from companies in China, but is ahead of all U.S.-based open models. The model preview’s strongest results come in cybersecurity tasks.

  • On the Intelligence Index, a weighted average of 10 evaluations of math, science, coding, and reasoning, Mistral Large 4 set to reasoning (38, $1.13 per task) ties GPT-6 Luna (38, $0.07) and trails three cheaper open weights models: MiMo-V2.6-Pro (46, $0.13), GLM-5.3-Flash (42, $0.25), and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash set to max reasoning (39, $0.27).
  • On Artificial Analysis’ Cyber Index, which measures models’ abilities to find and fix security vulnerabilities in code repositories, Mistral Large 4 set to reasoning (50 percent, $2.79 per task) ties GLM-5.3-Flash set to reasoning (50, $0.32) and trails only Grok 4.7 set to xhigh reasoning (56, $11.67) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro set to reasoning (56, $0.18) among publicly available models. The Daybreak Blue version of GPT-6 Sol at max reasoning, available only to organizations selected by OpenAI, tops the list with a 69 percent success rate at $1.77 per task.
  • On one component test of the Cyber Index, CyberGym-E2E-AA (tasks related to memory-safety bugs in popular open-source C and C++ projects), Mistral Large 4 solved 82 percent of tasks, the highest score among publicly available models, behind only GPT-6 Sol Daybreak Blue at max reasoning (93).

Behind the news: Mistral’s flagship models have alternated between closed and open weights and have been sometimes more and sometimes less competitive with top proprietary models. The company introduced Mistral Large, a proprietary model, in early 2024. Mistral Large 2 followed in July 2024 with weights licensed for research and non-commercial use; at the time, Mistral Large 2 was competitive with OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 3. In December 2025, Mistral released Mistral Large 3 under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, along with smaller Ministral 3 models, which the company built by repeatedly pruning and distilling the larger model.

Why it matters: The most capable open weights models on popular benchmarks are from companies based in China. Developers in the United States and Europe are trying to compete: In the U.S. Nvidia, Reflection AI, and Thinking Machines Lab, among others, have made progress, but Mistral remains the leading European lab. All of these companies pitch their models to organizations that want AI they can better control, whether via further post-training or greater trust they will be able to access the models regardless of geopolitics. Companies and governments all over the world, from South Korea to Saudi Arabia to Mexico, would prefer not to depend on either the United States or China for their access to intelligence. As Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch said earlier this year: “If you treat intelligence as electricity, then you just want to make sure that your access to intelligence cannot be throttled.”

We’re thinking: If you need AI sovereignty, and some industries and nations do, the best kind is running an open weights model on your own hardware. It doesn’t matter where a model was built (the U.S., Europe, China, or elsewhere) if your data and the model’s weights are entirely under your control.

Computers Built for Local AI

Developers have warmed to the economics and security of local models, either as an alternative or a complement to the cloud. Specialized computers from Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia aim to take a bite out of the AI market with machines capable of running larger and more capable open models on-device. 

What’s new: Apple’s upgraded Mac mini and Mac Studio desktops enable developers and AI researchers to run and fine-tune local models faster than before, offering an alternative to cloud computing for certain tasks. Nvidia’s DGX Spark series and Microsoft’s Surface Ultra laptops target a similar market: customers who want enough power to build with AI on their local machines, but in a user-friendly package.

How it works: By avoiding per-token cloud or monthly LLM subscription costs, a local setup could potentially save developers money over time, particularly [those running always-on agents]. But genuinely capable hardware is expensive: A maxed-out Mac Studio with 256GB of memory, an 80-core GPU, and 16TB of storage costs $18,299. For those with more modest local agent needs, a Mac mini starts at $899.

  • Developers and hobbyists have always used local machines to run (and in some cases train) smaller AI models. They’ve repurposed machines with expensive GPUs designed for gaming, video rendering, or cryptocurrency mining. Those are gradually being replaced by computers custom-built for local AI. Others build their own custom computers with server-grade GPUs and memory.
  • Apple’s Macs use custom-designed chips that integrate general-purpose CPUs, GPUs, and specialized neural processing units (NPUs) for machine-learning workloads. Notably, they use Apple Silicon rather than Nvidia’s popular GPUs, and they run Mac OS X rather than Windows or Linux.
  • Nvidia’s DGX Spark machines use a similar system-on-a-chip design, with Nvidia-designed CPUs, GPUs, and unified memory. Likewise, Microsoft uses Nvidia’s DGX Spark chips for its Surface Ultra laptops. Nvidia’s chips (whether in its own machines or Microsoft’s) max out at 128 GB of memory, with up to a 6144-core GPU. A top-of-the-line Surface Ultra laptop costs $5,899, but has a much smaller hard drive (only 1 TB) than the most expensive Mac Studio.
  • Traditionally, memory has been a bottleneck to running AI models locally. Large models require huge amounts of data to be moved between the CPU and GPU. Apple’s and Nvidia’s unified memory architecture aims to address that bottleneck by giving the processors access to the same pool of memory, reducing the need to copy data back and forth.

Performance: Apple Silicon and Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips were recently tested by an independent website, but most scores are self-reported.

  • The website Tom’s Hardware compared Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, a maxed-out MacBook Pro with an M5 Max processor, and AMD’s AI Ryzen Halo mini-PC. On the AgentPerf-Local benchmark, using a quantized version the popular open model Qwen 3.8-27B, the Surface Laptop Ultra was able to solve all problems within 18.9 minutes, faster than either the Mac (24.74) or the AI Ryzen Halo (42.1). The Surface Laptop Ultra with Nvidia hardware likewise outperformed Apple and AMD chips on AgentPerf-Local using Qwen 3.6 35B A3B (8.08 minutes to 10.12 and 13.29, respectively).
  • Apple says that the Mac mini with an M6 chip delivers AI performance up to 4x faster and graphics and storage 2x faster than its previous-generated M4 Mac mini. The Mac Studio with an M5 Ultra chip has 4.3x faster AI performance and up to 1.8x faster graphics than the previous Mac studio M3 Ultra.
  • Nvidia says its RTA Spark N1 chip gives comparable AI performance to an RTX 5070-class GPU. This gives it a processing power of 1 petaflop (1,000 teraflops) at FP4 precision, a common quantization for local AI models.
  • In general, Apple’s CPUs perform better, but Nvidia’s GPUs outperform Apple’s. Nvidia chips also give those developing or fine-tuning their own models access to Nvidia’s CUDA software, which helps AI models run on any Nvidia GPU.

Behind the news: Professionals using local AI inference are still a small market compared to the cloud, but now large enough to have genuine competition for computers designed for them at a wide range of price points. Mac desktops have sold well since the emergence of open-source personal agents, with news outlets describing weeks-long waits for Macs with more than 24GB of RAM as early as February. Nvidia’s DGX Spark laptops and desktops aim to similarly serve Windows users. For Nvidia, entering the desktop chip market ensures it can continue to sell its products to both consumer and enterprise markets, but also to increasingly blur that distinction. For Apple, it’s an alternative way to capitalize on the AI boom rather than building and hosting models, one that plays to its strengths in manufacturing high-end consumer hardware.

Why it matters: On-device AI models have several advantages over cloud-based models besides cost: more customizability, privacy, data sovereignty, potentially lower latency, and the ability to run without an internet connection. Others see cloud models and local models as complementary, designing workflows where a more powerful proprietary model solves high-level problems, then hands more mechanical work to a low-cost local model.

We’re thinking: We argued back in 2023 that strong commercial interests would increase AI usage at the edge. Not every application needs a frontier model, especially if a mid-sized model is fine-tuned to the task. But the main attraction today for local AI are privacy and data sovereignty, which is increasingly important as AI models handle more sensitive workloads. It’s useful for all of us to have a wide range of options.

Data Mixing, Minus the Guesswork

When you’re building a fine-tuning dataset, finding a mix of subject domains that yields a high-performing model can require expensive trial and error, because fine-tuned performance also depends on the quality of the individual examples. A cause-and-effect approach aims to separate the two effects.

What's new: Researchers at Tsinghua University, Ant Group, and Renmin University of China, with Zinan Tang and Yukun Zhang as lead authors, built CausalMix, a method for choosing the share of training examples drawn from various domains regardless of their quality.

Key insight: Datasets can be analyzed according to their data mixture (the proportions of examples that represent different domains) and data quality (variations among examples in difficulty, reasoning complexity, and/or composition). Data mixture and data quality correlate, and finding their correlation in any given dataset makes it possible to differentiate their separate impacts on the performance of a model trained on the dataset. Given a dataset and a consistent training budget, to find the marginal gain of its data mixture — that is, its effect on a fine-tuned model’s performance — we can subtract the effect of data quality from the model’s performance overall. The best data mixture is the one that yields the largest marginal gain. 

How it works: The authors compiled 512 subsets of 100,000 examples each drawn from the Tulu 3 dataset. Each subset contained examples for instruction following, coding, math, knowledge, and safety in different proportions. In addition, the authors measured data quality with respect to difficulty, reasoning complexity, and writing clarity as computed by OpenDataArena-Tool. They fine-tuned a separate Qwen2.5-0.5B model on each subset and recorded each fine-tuned model’s performance on 10 benchmarks. Then they trained three models, all of them ensembles of decision trees: one to estimate the portion of each Qwen2.5-0.5B’s performance attributable to data quality, one to estimate the portion of a data mixture that correlates with the corresponding data quality, and one to represent the effect of the data mixture on fine-tuned performance.
